datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate test loss on a similarly prepared sample; the paper does not specify the sample size or split. Loss is cross-entropy in nats, averaged over tokens in a 1024-token context.

baselines.name: LSTM
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained with the same dataset and context length as the Transformers; compared as a function of non-embedding parameter count. The paper does not say compute was equal.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with standard Transformers as a function of non-embedding parameter count; the paper notes that recurrent models reuse parameters and incur additional compute per parameter.

metrics.name: Cross-entropy loss (nats)
metrics.caveat: The paper cautions that continued improvement in loss may not translate to improvement on relevant language tasks, and smooth loss changes may mask qualitative capability changes; it does not report task scores instead.

confounds.name: Apparent scaling could be due to model shape rather than parameter count
confounds.detail: Differences in depth, width, attention heads, or feed-forward dimension could account for performance differences attributed to scale.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Vary shape hyperparameters while holding non-embedding parameter count approximately fixed; the reported loss varies only a few percent across a wide range of shapes.

confounds.name: The apparent scaling trend could be an artifact of counting embedding parameters or model depth
confounds.detail: Including vocabulary and positional embeddings could make performance appear to depend on depth in addition to model size.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare trends using total parameter count and non-embedding parameter count; models of different depths converge to a single trend when embeddings are excluded.

confounds.name: Finite-data overfitting could explain loss differences attributed to model or dataset scaling
confounds.detail: A model’s test loss might reflect overfitting rather than the proposed scaling relation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure test loss while varying model size and dataset size, stop when test loss ceases to decrease, and compare finite-dataset loss with the full-WebText2 result used as the infinite-data reference. The authors also acknowledge that regularization was not optimized across dataset and model sizes.

evidence_standards.name: Random-seed loss variation of roughly 0.02
evidence_standards.detail: The paper uses this estimated variation as a threshold for judging whether loss differences are meaningful for avoiding overfitting; it does not report a seed count, confidence interval, or statistical test.

metrics.name: Deadweight Compute Loss (DCL)
metrics.caveat: Measures excess FLOPs relative to the budget that would achieve the same loss under optimal allocation; the paper also reports DCL as a fraction of budget and, for empirical Llama 3, a dollar-cost range.

metrics.name: Relative error in compute-optimal token allocation (D*)
metrics.caveat: The sign indicates direction: negative means underestimation and positive means overestimation. The paper examines errors across compute budgets and sampling-grid widths.

metrics.name: Relative error in scaling exponents
metrics.caveat: Typical error alone can obscure sporadic large optimizer failures; the paper reports maximum absolute errors alongside geometric-mean absolute relative errors.

metrics.name: Geometric mean absolute relative error
metrics.caveat: Can obscure consequential outliers; the paper reports maximum absolute relative error alongside it.

metrics.name: Maximum absolute relative error
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside typical accuracy because sporadic optimizer failures in a minority of fits are considered practically consequential.

metrics.name: Estimator variance for the compute-optimal exponent
metrics.caveat: Used as a precision comparison under the stated unbiased, symmetric, perfectly centered conditions; lower variance is better.

metrics.name: Dollar cost
metrics.caveat: Cost estimates assume 50% H100 model-FLOPs utilization and $2 per H100-hour; empirical-row ranges are reported as 90% bootstrap confidence intervals.

controls.name: Symmetric loss surface with perfectly centered sampling
controls.detail: Noise-free Approach 2 simulations use α=β and sampling grids centered on the true optimum; the paper establishes this as its baseline before changing surface asymmetry or sampling conditions.
controls.rules_out: That the observed Approach 2 errors occur even under ideal symmetric, perfectly centered conditions; the comparison isolates errors associated with asymmetry or sampling placement.

controls.name: Synthetic Llama 3 condition
controls.detail: Generate IsoFLOP data from the Llama 3 surface with the specified sampling bias, then compare its allocation error with the empirical fit to digitized Llama 3 data.
controls.rules_out: That the empirical Llama 3 misallocation is explained solely by the modeled systematic sampling bias; the simulation estimates the bias contribution under that controlled setup.

confounds.name: The errors could be caused by noise rather than structural bias
confounds.detail: If noise alone explained the errors, the headline bias would not establish a systematic failure of the parabolic approximation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Noise-free synthetic simulations with known surfaces and ideal sampling show intercept bias on asymmetric surfaces; the paper also reports that the biases persist in noisy comparisons.

confounds.name: Residual noise may vary across compute budgets, undermining the assumed uniform Gaussian noise model
confounds.detail: Budget-dependent residual variance could make the simulated noise treatment an inadequate explanation of real-data behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Examine residual variance across compute budgets in six real IsoFLOP experiments; the paper reports no strong evidence that variance differs by budget in most experiments.

confounds.name: The empirical Llama 3 misallocation could reflect the actual experiment design rather than the modeled systematic biases
confounds.detail: The empirical result alone does not separate bias attributable to the actual Llama 3 IsoFLOP data from bias under the paper's controlled sampling assumptions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Fit a simulated Llama 3 condition designed to isolate the modeled experiment-design biases; it yields 0.2% DCL versus 6.5% for the empirical comparison.

confounds.name: The assumed Chinchilla loss-surface form may be incorrect in practice
confounds.detail: If the true loss surface differs from L(N,D)=E+A/N^α+B/D^β, conclusions based on fitting that form may not apply.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper explicitly lists correctness of the Chinchilla loss surface as an assumption and acknowledges alternative surface forms.

confounds.name: Published studies' sampling pathologies may be characterized incorrectly or over-quantified
confounds.detail: The visual signs of asymmetry and off-center or drifting sampling in published IsoFLOP curves do not by themselves quantify the resulting errors precisely.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not quantitatively ruled out; the paper characterizes these issues qualitatively and acknowledges that they are difficult to quantify precisely.

evidence_standards.name: 256 independent noise realizations per configuration
evidence_standards.detail: The noisy exponent comparison repeats each configuration 256 times; results are summarized with geometric-mean absolute relative error and min-to-max ranges, with maximum errors also emphasized. No statistical significance test or tie margin is specified.

evidence_standards.name: 10 trials per configuration
evidence_standards.detail: The symmetric-surface variance comparison uses 10 trials per configuration and reports estimator variance; no statistical significance test or tie margin is specified.

evidence_standards.name: 90% bootstrap confidence intervals for empirical cost ranges
evidence_standards.detail: The empirical rows' dollar-cost ranges are reported as 90% bootstrap confidence intervals; the paper does not specify a general threshold for declaring differences real.

(2026b) dataset. Chinchilla, Quanta, and SoftQ use the same Huber objective with threshold 10^-3 on log-loss residuals.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the other scaling laws on the same baseline data and fit diagnostics; uses the same Huber objective with threshold 10^-3 on log-loss residuals as Chinchilla and SoftQ.

baselines.name: Muennighoff-style scaling law
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same baseline data and fit diagnostics. The main comparison fits base Chinchilla coefficients on the same split, holds them fixed, and fits only the decay constants R_N* and R_D*.

metrics.name: Validation loss
metrics.caveat: dLLM validation loss is a negative evidence lower bound (an upper bound on negative log-likelihood), whereas AR loss is exact negative log-likelihood; the paper cautions that a slightly higher dLLM value does not imply worse performance.

metrics.name: Zero-shot accuracy (acc and acc_norm)
metrics.caveat: The paper treats downstream evaluations as a coarse capability check at this academic scale; gains are mixed across tasks and are described as directionally agreeing with validation-loss improvements.

metrics.name: Token-level loss gap
metrics.caveat: The paper removes the center region |Δℓ|<1 when showing gap tails; it reports the fractions with Δℓ≥1 and Δℓ≤−1 to argue the gain is not due to a few isolated outliers.

metrics.name: SSE-based Gaussian AIC
metrics.caveat: Lower is better; the paper reports it alongside RMSE and MAE for scaling-law comparisons.

metrics.name: Unique-data efficiency ratio (U_eq/U_MIR)
metrics.caveat: The estimate depends on the selected baseline scaling law; the paper notes that SoftQ gives the most conservative ratio at 400M among the laws compared.

controls.name: Strongly regularized AR without MIR
controls.detail: The unmodified AR recipe uses the same architecture, optimizer, and per-cell-tuned epochs, weight decay, and learning rate as MIR; it omits only the auxiliary masked-input loss.
controls.rules_out: A validation-loss difference attributable merely to changing the other training settings; the comparison isolates the added MIR loss.

confounds.name: The reported dLLM advantage over AR is due to insufficient AR regularization
confounds.detail: If weak AR regularization explains the gap, it would not establish a distinct advantage from random masking once AR is strongly regularized.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare multi-epoch AR and dLLM at weight decay 0.1, then compare strongly regularized AR with dLLM using the AR-tuned weight decay; the strongly regularized recipes have comparable validation losses across 140M, 257M, and 664M.

confounds.name: MIR’s validation-loss gain is driven by a few isolated token outliers
confounds.detail: A small number of extreme token improvements could account for the aggregate loss difference without a broad improvement.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Analyze token-level loss gaps on the 1.4B DCLM models: after removing |Δℓ|<1, 6.61% of tokens favor MIR by at least 1 and 5.41% favor the baseline by at least 1; the paper interprets the larger MIR-better tail as evidence of a broad effect.

confounds.name: MIR’s benefit is specific to natural-language DCLM data
confounds.detail: The DCLM result alone would not show that the benefit transfers to a different data distribution.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on code-heavy Stack-V2 with hyperparameters tuned only on DCLM; MIR lowers validation loss at all five model sizes.

confounds.name: SoftQ’s stronger scaling-law fit reflects in-sample fit rather than predictive performance
confounds.detail: A better fit to the points used to estimate a law would not by itself establish that the law predicts unseen data or transfers to another dataset.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Fit on the 100M/200M/300M points and predict the five held-out 400M points, and also compare full-fit performance on the independent Kim et al. (2026b) dataset.

evidence_standards.name: Five random seeds for DCLM validation-loss comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports means over five seeds and error bars of one standard deviation; it also says MIR improves validation loss for every matched seed at every model scale.

evidence_standards.name: Reported downstream evaluation uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: The downstream table reports ± values for its metrics, but the paper does not specify in the provided text what those values represent or give a statistical test or significance threshold.

evidence_standards.name: Scaling-law fit and prediction protocol
evidence_standards.detail: For Chinchilla, Quanta, and SoftQ, fit with Huber loss using threshold 10^-3 on log-loss residuals; report raw-scale RMSE and MAE and SSE-based Gaussian AIC. Include a held-out 400M prediction test and a full fit on the independent Kim et al. (2026b) dataset.

metrics.name: Average top-1 error
metrics.caveat: Individual downstream-task predictions are significantly noisier than the average; the paper reports individual-task errors alongside the average over the 17 evaluations.

metrics.name: Relative prediction error
metrics.caveat: The paper does not state a caveat; it reports the relative error as |prediction − ground truth| / ground truth for predicted loss or average top-1 error.

confounds.name: The downstream prediction result could depend on selecting tasks with above-chance signal rather than reflect reliable aggregate scaling
confounds.detail: The 17-task subset is selected so at least one 0.154B model is at least 10 percentage points above chance on each evaluation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports evaluation-set ablations in Appendix F and says including tasks such as MMLU, where performance is near chance, does not invalidate the results.

evidence_standards.name: Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: The paper shows shaded bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for fitted trends. It does not specify a seed count, statistical test, or numerical margin for calling two results equivalent.

datasets.name: BookCorpus
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to train five language models with total parameter counts 0.8M, 1.6M, 2.1M, 3.3M, and 4.6M. GPT-2 tokenizer (vocabulary 50,257), context length 16; training-token budgets 262M for the first three models and 524M for the last two. Scaling coefficients were fitted with Chinchilla’s Method 1 using C=6ND. No dataset split or separate evaluation-scoring procedure is stated.

metrics.name: Compute-optimal parameter scaling coefficient a in N* ∝ C^a
metrics.caveat: The fitted coefficient changes with parameter/compute accounting and model-size range; the paper reports total-parameter/compute and non-embedding-parameter/compute results separately and notes that the latter relationship is not generally a power law.

metrics.name: Compute-optimal data scaling coefficient b in D* ∝ C^b
metrics.caveat: Under the paper’s C=6ND approximation, b is implied by a as 1−a; it is not an independent coefficient.

metrics.name: Compute-loss scaling exponent γ
metrics.caveat: The fitted exponent depends on using total versus non-embedding compute, the model-size range, and whether the compute-loss form includes an offset; the paper compares both forms and reports the offset-based Chinchilla form alongside Kaplan’s no-offset form.

controls.name: Scheme 1: shared learning rate, no annealing
controls.detail: One learning rate (0.001) for all model sizes; one model per size and no annealing, compared with the per-model best-learning-rate condition.
controls.rules_out: A shared learning rate alone explaining the parameter-scaling coefficient obtained under the other tested conditions; the coefficient still differs only modestly across optimization schemes.

controls.name: Scheme 3: per-model best learning rate with single cosine annealing
controls.detail: One model per size, with cosine annealing at the update budget; compared with Scheme 2 and Scheme 4.
controls.rules_out: The use of a single cosine decay, by itself, explaining the large coefficient difference attributed to parameter-counting basis.

controls.name: Scheme 4: per-model best learning rate with multiple cosine-annealed budgets
controls.detail: Six models per size at budgets 0.25D, 0.5D, 0.75D, 1.0D, 1.5D, and 2.0D, with cosine annealing; compared with the single-model conditions.
controls.rules_out: Multiple training budgets and cosine schedules being necessary to obtain the reported compute-parameter coefficient; Scheme 2 gives the same coefficient.

confounds.name: Optimization-scheme differences between Kaplan and Chinchilla explain the coefficient discrepancy
confounds.detail: The headline coefficient difference could arise from learning-rate choice, annealing, or multiple training budgets rather than parameter/compute accounting and scale.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares four small-scale optimization schemes varying shared versus per-model learning rates, no annealing versus cosine annealing, and single versus multiple budgets. It reports only marginal coefficient changes across these schemes, with Scheme 2 matching Scheme 4; this does not test every optimization difference, including differing warmup schedules.

confounds.name: Different datasets explain the discrepancy
confounds.detail: Kaplan used OpenWebText2 and Chinchilla used MassiveText, so dataset differences could produce different scaling coefficients without the paper’s proposed accounting-and-scale explanation being sufficient.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out by a direct cross-dataset experiment; the paper acknowledges dataset differences as a limitation.

confounds.name: Other study-design differences explain some of the discrepancy
confounds.detail: Differences in transformer details, tokenizers, vocabulary sizes, positional embeddings, warmup schedules, hyperparameter tuning, or compute counting could affect the published coefficients independently of the proposed explanation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out comprehensively. The paper tests some optimization-scheme variations at tiny scale and argues they have a smaller effect, but acknowledges the remaining differences as limitations.

confounds.name: Mixture rankings may change with model size or training-token count

confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure validation MAE as the number of fitting mixtures and training domains vary, and compare implicit aggregation across different numbers of implicit domains with explicit aggregation; the paper reports low errors when the implicit-domain count is at least the actual count, including larger counts.

Neural scaling-law fit parameters (E, A, α, B, β)
Compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio

confounds.name: Ambiguity in which model parameter counts are used
confounds.detail: The reported counts and counts computed from the architecture using alternative formulas differ, potentially changing the scaling-law estimates and compute-optimal ratio.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Refit using reported, standard-formula, and best-fit-formula counts; the fit parameters and ratio remain broadly similar.

confounds.name: Multiplicative error in model parameter counts

confounds.ruled_out_by: Sweep multiplicative factors and refit; the ratio remains approximately constant across compute, though its level shifts.

confounds.name: Additive error in model parameter counts, such as including or excluding embedding parameters

confounds.ruled_out_by: Sweep positive and negative additive offsets and refit; the paper finds that they can change the ratio’s trend, so this possibility is measured but not ruled out.

confounds.name: Size-dependent systematic bias in model parameter counts
confounds.detail: Bias that affects smaller and larger models differently could change the fitted exponent and the compute dependence of the optimal ratio.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Sweep the systematic-bias parameter and refit; the paper finds that this can make the ratio less constant, so this possibility is measured but not ruled out.

confounds.name: Noise in model parameter counts
confounds.detail: Noisy parameter counts could make fitted scaling-law estimates and the optimal ratio uncertain or unstable.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Add log-normal noise at varying strengths and refit; uncertainty increases substantially and high noise can produce NaNs, so this possibility is measured but not ruled out.

metrics.name: Cross-entropy loss
metrics.caveat: Test-loss evaluations can be noisy; in test-to-test prediction the evaluation noise affects both axes. The paper notes train loss is a lower-variance input and reports train-to-test predictions alongside test-to-test predictions. It uses loss rather than accuracy for downstream tasks, noting accuracy is a harder metric that can hide smooth progress until performance rises above random chance.

metrics.name: Relative error
metrics.caveat: Defined as |predicted − actual| / actual for the extrapolation run’s test loss; no additional caveat is stated.

confounds.name: Errors in estimating irreducible entropy could explain fit or extrapolation failures
confounds.detail: The paper says estimating asymptotic entropy is fundamentally difficult and hypothesizes that poor estimates often explain failed fits or extrapolations, rather than the loss-to-loss relationship itself failing.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No specific measurement is reported to rule this out; the authors acknowledge it as a limitation.

confounds.name: Noisy trends may indicate that the shifted power law does not hold globally
confounds.detail: The paper says some train-to-test and test-to-test fits are noisy, especially at high losses, and that this could be more than evaluation noise.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No measurement distinguishes noise from a breakdown of the power-law trend; the authors explicitly leave this unresolved.

datasets.name: TinyStories
datasets.eval_protocol: Train models from scratch on P-token slices; measure n-gram loss as a function of context horizon and training-token count, and autoregressive loss across context lengths. The paper does not specify an evaluation split or preprocessing.

datasets.name: WikiText-103
datasets.eval_protocol: Train models from scratch on P-token slices; measure n-gram loss as a function of context horizon and training-token count, and autoregressive loss across context lengths. Estimate token correlations from the full training set. The paper does not specify an evaluation split or preprocessing.

metrics.name: n-gram loss (L_n)
metrics.caveat: It is an upper bound on conditional entropy and can depend on model class and training amount; the paper uses convergence with increasing P and agreement across model classes as evidence that it estimates the dataset quantity.

metrics.name: autoregressive loss (L_AR)
metrics.caveat: At fixed context length T, the prediction horizon can eventually approach T and truncate the predicted scaling regime; small-P points for large T are also harder to optimize. The paper compares curves across T and fits the lower envelope.

metrics.name: conditional-entropy decay exponent (gamma)
metrics.caveat: Raw conditional entropies are computationally infeasible to estimate from counts at the vocabulary sizes and horizons considered, so the paper fits the initial decay of L_n for the largest-P model and checks convergence across P and model classes.

metrics.name: token-correlation decay exponent (beta)
metrics.caveat: WikiText correlations are better described by a broken power law, so the paper fits the short-lag regime n<=32 relevant to its P range; it excludes a localized peak around n≈10 from the coarse-grained fit. The Frobenius norm tracks the operator norm closely.

metrics.name: data-limited scaling exponent (alpha_D)
metrics.caveat: Empirical fits are limited by small-P optimization at large T and by finite-T truncation at large P. The paper fits the first m points of the lower envelope across T and reports bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

confounds.name: The estimated conditional-entropy decay is an artifact of the model architecture or finite training data
confounds.detail: Conditional entropy is estimated using trained-model n-gram losses rather than raw context counts, so model-specific or insufficient-data behavior could produce the apparent exponent.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports convergence of n-gram loss curves with increasing P and agreement across GPT-2-style models with absolute or rotary positional embeddings, LLaMA-style models, infini-gram, and Mamba.

confounds.name: Within-horizon optimization, rather than an expanding useful prediction horizon, drives the scaling result
confounds.detail: The autoregressive loss could improve mainly because models become better at using contexts already within their effective horizon, rather than because more distant token dependencies become usable.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For n<=12, the paper examines the large-P n-gram-loss tails after horizon-related saturation, fits their decay to an asymptote, and reports that the resulting exponents delta_n exceed gamma/(2 beta).

confounds.name: Finite context length or optimization at small P produces the apparent autoregressive scaling exponent
confounds.detail: A fixed T can truncate the regime when n*(P) approaches T, while large-T runs are harder to optimize at small P.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares learning curves across T, identifies the regime with n*(P)<<T, and estimates empirical exponents from the lower envelope across T; it also acknowledges that the tested scaling range is finite.

evidence_standards.name: Bootstrap uncertainty estimates for language-statistic exponents
evidence_standards.detail: The paper obtains errors on gamma and beta by bootstrapping.

evidence_standards.name: Uncertainty propagation and bootstrap confidence intervals for scaling exponents
evidence_standards.detail: The predicted alpha_D uncertainty is obtained by standard propagation of uncertainty. Empirical alpha_D is fitted from the first m points of the lower envelope across T, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; the paper reports overlap with the predicted range for up to 10 of 12 points on TinyStories and all 8 points on WikiText.

controls.name: Random data
controls.detail: Models trained on randomly sampled data are compared with models trained on selected or synthetic data; the random-data condition uses 8B tokens, compared with 7B selected and 2B synthetic tokens.
controls.rules_out: Provides a random-data reference for the refined-data results, but the differing token counts mean the comparison does not isolate data refinement from token quantity.

evidence_standards.name: More than 200 training runs; bootstrapped standard errors for fitted constants
evidence_standards.detail: Table 1 reports 210 data points for the paper's estimates and standard errors obtained by bootstrapping. The paper does not state a significance test, seed-based variance rule, or margin for treating results as ties.

datasets.name: multitask sparse parity
datasets.eval_protocol: Synthetic binary-classification task with 500 subtasks, n=100 task bits, k=3, and α=0.4; task bits are uniform and active control-bit indices follow a Zipf distribution proportional to i^-(α+1). Report cross-entropy test loss and loss by subtask. For data scaling, train on dataset sizes from 10^4 to 5×10^6, use a sufficiently wide network, train for multiple epochs, and record performance at the lowest mean test loss (early stopping). For parameter and step scaling, use online batches and train for 2×10^5 steps; hidden-layer widths range from 10 to 500.

datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate Pythia models on approximately 10 million tokens from The Pile test set; record cross-entropy loss on every token. The paper does not specify further preprocessing.

metrics.name: mean test cross-entropy loss
metrics.caveat: An aggregate loss can smooth over abrupt changes on individual subtasks; the paper also reports loss by subtask. For language models, near-zero-loss tokens are common but contribute little to mean loss, which is dominated by higher-loss tokens; the paper also examines the per-token loss distribution p(L) and its loss-weighted form Lp(L).

metrics.name: parameter-scaling exponent α_N
metrics.caveat: For Pythia, the 6.4b model does not fit the scaling curve, so the reported exponent is measured from the first six models only.

metrics.name: QDG cluster rank-frequency slope
metrics.caveat: The estimate depends on clustering choices and is uncertain because clustering can be biased and gradients noisy. The paper measures the envelope of curves from varying cluster counts over ranks 100–1000, reports a slope of approximately −1.24, and estimates uncertainty of at least 0.2.

confounds.name: Apparent sharp per-token transitions may be noise rather than genuine discrete emergence
confounds.detail: A sharp loss drop at one model scale could arise from variation across random initializations rather than an underlying discrete quantum.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors say multiple random-seed runs at each scale would be needed to test this, and they did not report them.

confounds.name: Scaling may be a smooth process rather than learning discrete quanta
confounds.detail: The observed scaling behavior could occur without an underlying discreteness in what models learn.

confounds.name: QDG cluster frequencies may reflect clustering artifacts rather than quantum-use frequencies
confounds.detail: Gradient noise and clustering bias could produce apparent cluster-size power laws even if they do not reflect the true frequency distribution of skills.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: Appendix E finds similar-looking curves in a toy model of the clustering process when dimension and noise are high, and the authors describe the measured exponent as highly uncertain.

confounds.name: QDG clusters may group samples by output token rather than by a coherent skill
confounds.detail: Clusters with the same predicted token might not represent a shared prediction rule or skill.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors manually inspect clusters and report that they usually share a coherent reason for predicting the token, rather than being based merely on having the same output.

evidence_standards.name: Toy-task seed handling
evidence_standards.detail: For data-scaling experiments, the same seed and model size are used across runs. The authors report that parameter-scaling results are noisier, possibly because initialization affects which quanta are learned.

evidence_standards.name: Random-seed evidence for per-token emergence
evidence_standards.detail: No multiple-seed comparison is reported for each model scale; the authors explicitly say this is needed to determine whether sharp transitions are genuine or noise.

evidence_standards.name: Uncertainty for QDG frequency exponent
evidence_standards.detail: The authors estimate uncertainty of at least 0.2 for the rank-frequency slope and treat the measured slope of approximately −1.24 as compatible with the expected −1.08 within that uncertainty.

evidence_standards.name: Pythia scaling-exponent fit
evidence_standards.detail: The reported parameter-scaling exponent is fitted using the first six models; the 6.4b model is excluded because it does not fit the scaling curve.

Interpolation testing uses s=8; extrapolation uses s=12 plus extensions, and supplementary test sets use s∈[1,19]. The paper reports loss and accuracy by difficulty; it notes that the online-training setup may leave interpolation-test duplicates, while extrapolation tests must be deduplicated.

metrics.name: Autoregressive cross-entropy loss
metrics.caveat: The entropy-plus-KL interpretation relies on the model being able to represent the data distribution in the infinite-data/compute limit; for deterministic math answers, the true entropy should vanish, so the interpretation differs. The paper also cautions that the largest models in some model-size trends are not fully converged.

metrics.name: ImageNet classification loss
metrics.caveat: The generative loss approaching its irreducible level does not imply downstream classification returns are diminishing; the paper reports classification loss and error rate alongside generative-loss trends.

metrics.name: ImageNet classification error rate (1 − accuracy)
metrics.caveat: The paper reports classification loss alongside error rate; it finds both continue to scale smoothly even where generative loss approaches its irreducible level.

metrics.name: Math-problem accuracy
metrics.caveat: Accuracy is reported alongside answer-token loss; the paper emphasizes that extrapolation performance at fixed training loss is nearly the same across model sizes.

metrics.name: Empirical mutual information between text and image
metrics.caveat: Blank captions or images can be out of distribution and inflate the estimate; the paper measures it after fine-tuning on a mixture containing blank-caption or blank-image examples.

metrics.name: Infogain (mutual information divided by text loss)
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that text and images are not always closely correlated and that infogain grows slowly with model size; it reports mutual information alongside the ratio.

controls.name: Randomly initialized ImageNet classifier trained from scratch
controls.detail: An equivalent Transformer is trained only on the classification task, without generative pretraining, and compared with fine-tuned generative models.
controls.rules_out: A classification gain that would occur just as well without generative pretraining.

controls.name: Text-to-image training from scratch on a 95/5 multimodal/blank-caption mixture
controls.detail: The paper compares this condition with the mutual-information measurement after fine-tuning on a mixture of paired and blank-caption data.
controls.rules_out: That the reported text-to-image mutual-information result is specific to the fine-tuning procedure used to address blank captions being out of distribution.

confounds.name: Blank captions or images are out of distribution
confounds.detail: If the model has only trained on multimodal data, losses on blank-caption or blank-image inputs may be atypical and make the estimated mutual information too large; the paper reports estimates about twice as large without the correction.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper fine-tunes for 10^4 steps on an even mixture of paired and blank-caption data for text-to-image, or paired and blank-image data for image-to-text, before measuring mutual information. Text-to-image training from scratch on a 95/5 multimodal/blank-caption mixture gave similar results.

confounds.name: Image scaling trends are an artifact of overfitting
confounds.detail: A train/test gap could make test-loss scaling appear to reflect generalization failure rather than the reported scaling behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports test loss and says it observed no train/test gap for the image and VQ-image models.

confounds.name: Compute-optimal trends reflect inefficient use of data or overly large batches
confounds.detail: If batches are above the critical batch size early in training, some compute may be wasted and the estimated optimal model-size trend could be affected.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper did not measure critical batch sizes or adjust compute estimates for them, and says this may warrant further study.

confounds.name: The apparent compute/data-size scaling inconsistency means one or more fitted trends break down
confounds.detail: The extrapolated compute-loss trend eventually crosses the dataset-size loss bound, so the reported trends cannot all continue unchanged.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out. The paper presents increasingly efficient optimization and learning curves approaching the dataset-size trend as a plausible hypothesis, and explicitly says the resolution is unknown.

confounds.name: Interpolation-test examples may overlap with online training data
confounds.detail: The paper cannot be sure that the s=8 interpolation tests are deduplicated from procedurally generated training problems.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out for interpolation; the paper says the extrapolation test must be deduplicated.

datasets.name: PCFG-generated token-sequence datasets
datasets.eval_protocol: Six synthetic datasets with varying grammar complexity; models of 4.2M, 8.8M, 20.3M, 59.0M, 275.3M, and 1.4B parameters are trained on 100K, 1M, 5M, 20M, 50M, or 100M tokens, and final losses are used to fit a scaling law. Documents are filled to the model context length by sampling sentences and truncating overflow; sentences are separated by token ID 0. No train/test split is specified. Additional PCFG sets hold terminal count fixed or approximately hold gzip-compressibility fixed.

datasets.name: Real-world code and natural-language datasets
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for gzip-compressibility analysis, not language-model scaling-law training: gzip is applied to a sample of 1,000 token sequences, with median and standard deviation of compressed-to-original size ratios reported. The paper does not name the specific datasets.

baselines.name: Chinchilla scaling law
baselines.fair_comparison: The Chinchilla frontier and the frontiers from the paper's fitted laws are computed using the same compute-optimal frontier formula; the paper does not specify further matching conditions.

metrics.name: gzip-compressibility
metrics.caveat: The proxy may be confounded by syntactic properties such as vocabulary size, and the paper notes that some features affecting scaling may not be modeled well by gzip-compressibility; it also reports fixed-vocabulary and approximately fixed-compressibility PCFG comparisons.

metrics.name: Fitted scaling-law parameters (E, A, B, α, β)

controls.name: Fixed-terminal-count PCFG comparison
controls.detail: Terminal count is held at 300 while non-terminals, RHS options, and RHS length vary across four PCFG datasets.
controls.rules_out: That the observed relationship between gzip-compressibility and scaling-law shifts is explained merely by vocabulary size; the shifts persist with terminal count held fixed.

controls.name: Approximately fixed-gzip-compressibility PCFG comparison
controls.detail: Syntactic properties are varied non-monotonically across PCFG datasets with gzip-compressibility approximately 0.32–0.40.
controls.rules_out: That varying those syntactic properties alone produces meaningful scaling-law shifts; the paper reports no meaningful shift, especially in α and A.

confounds.name: Vocabulary size or other syntactic properties, rather than gzip-compressibility, explain the scaling-law shifts
confounds.detail: A correlation between gzip-compressibility and fitted scaling-law parameters could arise because compressibility covaries with grammar properties such as vocabulary size.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper varies other syntactic properties while holding terminal count at 300 and finds scaling-law shifts persist; it also varies syntactic properties while keeping gzip-compressibility approximately 0.32–0.40 and reports no meaningful parameter shifts.

evidence_standards.name: Linear-regression p-values for scaling-law parameters versus gzip-compressibility
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports p-values for the fitted regressions and describes parameter trends with p<0.05 as significant. It does not specify seeds, repeated-run variance, confidence intervals, or another statistical test.

metrics.name: Mean squared error (MSE)
metrics.caveat: The paper says estimating marginal-variance-based R² can add noise when test sets are small; it uses MSE as the main evaluation measure because targets are normalized to [0,1].

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: Specific benchmarks can have limited dynamic range: some saturate for large models and others remain near random for small models. The paper uses PC-1 as a smoother, wider-dynamic-range capability measure alongside benchmark performance.

metrics.name: R²
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that estimating marginal variance in R² can add noise when test sets are small, and therefore uses MSE as its main holdout evaluation measure.

controls.name: Naive few-shot prompting
controls.detail: For the CoT comparison, models are evaluated with naive few-shot prompting rather than CoT prompting with eight reasoning examples; both are evaluated under greedy decoding.
controls.rules_out: That the predicted performance of the CoT condition is simply the performance of the same models without the CoT prompting intervention.

controls.name: Single sampled CoT answer
controls.detail: For the Self-Consistency comparison, the reference condition uses one sampled CoT answer, while Self-Consistency aggregates five sampled CoT paths at temperature 0.7.
controls.rules_out: That any CoT answer or sampling alone explains the difference attributed to aggregating multiple paths.

controls.name: Random model-subset selection
controls.detail: Randomly selected model subsets are compared with V-optimal subsets under the same subset budgets and prediction tasks.
controls.rules_out: That the V-optimal subset’s prediction accuracy is merely due to evaluating fewer models rather than the selection criterion.

confounds.name: Scaling-law construction or hyperparameter choices cause overfitting
confounds.detail: The headline prediction accuracy could reflect choices made when constructing the scaling laws rather than generalizable weak-to-strong prediction.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Systematic weaker-to-stronger holdouts; preprocessing, including PCA imputation, is fitted on training models only and applied to held-out models. The paper also preregistered predictions and evaluated them on models released later.

confounds.name: Apparent emergence is an artifact of too few scale points
confounds.detail: A rapid but smooth transition could look discontinuous when only a few models are evaluated.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper uses a higher-resolution set of models, fits sigmoidal scaling curves, and tests extrapolations from weaker models to stronger models.

confounds.name: Benchmark contamination
confounds.detail: Benchmark data leaking into model training could affect measured performance and the inferred scaling relationships.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in this paper; the authors explicitly state that their assumptions do not account for possible benchmark contamination.

confounds.name: Heterogeneity within model families
confounds.detail: Models within a family may have different compute efficiencies or scaling behaviors, which could undermine the assumed family-level compute-to-capability relationship.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in this paper; the authors explicitly acknowledge this as an assumption and a direction for future investigation.

evidence_standards.name: Weak-to-strong holdout validation
evidence_standards.detail: Fit on weaker models and evaluate extrapolated predictions on stronger held-out models; by default, the training cutoff is at or below Llama-2-7B FLOPs. Preprocessing is fitted on the training set only.

evidence_standards.name: Preregistered future-model predictions
evidence_standards.detail: The paper preregistered predictions and later assessed them on models released after the initial paper release.

evidence_standards.name: Decoding settings for post-training results
evidence_standards.detail: CoT comparisons are reported with greedy decoding; Self-Consistency samples five CoT paths at temperature 0.7 and aggregates their answers, with a single sampled CoT answer as comparator.

metrics.caveat: In data-mixing experiments, average validation loss can fail to reflect downstream performance changes when domain losses move in different directions; the paper reports domain-specific losses instead.

metrics.name: Domain-specific pre-training loss
metrics.caveat: For LMs trained on a fixed distribution, domain-specific losses are closely related and add no information; using them can increase error propagation and overfitting.

controls.name: Average-loss linear regression (FLP) in the data-mixing setting
controls.detail: Predicts downstream performance from average validation loss rather than domain-specific losses.
controls.rules_out: Whether FLP-M's improvement over this condition depends on using domain-specific loss rather than simply fitting a predictor in the data-mixing setting.

controls.name: Total-compute-only analytical form (M1)
controls.detail: Predicts domain loss using total compute, without separate terms for the general and code data sources.
controls.rules_out: Whether the data-source-specific terms improve domain-loss prediction over total compute alone.

controls.name: Separate-source compute form (M2) and weighted-compute form (M3)
controls.detail: Alternative FLOPs-to-loss analytical forms compared with FLP-M's M4 form.
controls.rules_out: Whether the selected M4 analytical form predicts domain-specific loss more accurately than these alternative forms.

controls.name: FLOPs-based performance prediction
controls.detail: Uses compute rather than pre-training loss as the input to downstream-performance prediction.
controls.rules_out: Whether performance prediction gains depend on using pre-training loss rather than directly mapping FLOPs to performance.

controls.name: Average-loss and domain-linear predictors
controls.detail: A linear regression on average loss and a linear combination of domain losses, compared with the domain-loss neural network.
controls.rules_out: Whether prediction gains depend on domain-specific inputs and the neural-network mapping rather than average loss or a linear mapping.

confounds.name: Training dynamics, rather than compute alone, determine downstream performance
confounds.detail: At a given FLOPs budget, performance can vary with model size, token count, and learning-rate schedule, so a FLOPs-to-performance fit may be unreliable without the claimed role for pre-training loss.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares FP and FLP using identical sampling LMs; FLP predicts target performance more accurately across the reported benchmarks.

confounds.name: Average validation loss can conceal capability changes caused by data mixtures
confounds.detail: A mixture change can increase code loss while decreasing general-data loss, leaving average loss similar even as downstream capabilities and performance change.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares FLP's average-loss predictor with FLP-M's domain-specific-loss predictor on mixed-data experiments; FLP-M predicts better overall.

confounds.name: Sparse sampling may explain the large TriviaQA prediction error
confounds.detail: The authors attribute FLP-M's 20–30% TriviaQA relative error to too few sampling points to characterize the accelerated performance improvement between under 1B and 3B.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper identifies the missing intermediate-scale sampling points as a limitation and suggests adding models between 1B and 3B.

evidence_standards.name: Above-random checkpoint inclusion threshold
evidence_standards.detail: For fitting the Loss-to-Performance curve, checkpoints are retained only if performance exceeds the random benchmark by at least 5.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: For Modus Tollens, every example has the same correct answer (“Yes”); the authors note that answer bias can therefore make accuracy jump between 100% and 0%. They report accuracy and identify the class imbalance as a limitation.

metrics.name: Classification loss
metrics.caveat: The paper does not state a specific caveat. It computes average negative log-probability of the correct answer, with probabilities over the provided answer options renormalized to sum to 1.

metrics.name: Sequence probability / loss
metrics.caveat: For Prompt Injection, loss can worsen because the model becomes more confident in incorrect answers, not only because it selects incorrect answers more often. The paper reports loss (and plots negated loss in Figure 4).

metrics.name: Human agreement
metrics.caveat: Used to check that task labels match human judgments; the paper reports agreement on random samples of at least 50 examples per task. No further caveat is stated.

confounds.name: Submissions may overfit to quirks of a particular model series
confounds.detail: An apparent inverse-scaling result could reflect idiosyncrasies of the model series used to select the task rather than a more robust scaling behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors evaluated on private Anthropic and DeepMind model series to check whether inverse scaling also appeared on held-out models.

confounds.name: Task labels may not match what humans consider correct
confounds.detail: A task could appear to show inverse scaling simply because its submitted answers are incorrect or misleading.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Crowdworkers checked random samples of at least 50 examples per task; they could use the internet to help determine answers. The paper reports human agreement for the tasks.

confounds.name: Grammatical errors in Modus Tollens examples could affect its result
confounds.detail: Errors in some examples could make the apparent scaling trend reflect faulty items rather than the intended reasoning task.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors removed the affected examples (less than 10% of the task) and report that this had very little effect on the results.

confounds.name: Modus Tollens accuracy may reflect class imbalance and answer bias
confounds.detail: All examples have “Yes” as the correct answer, so a model biased toward one answer can produce near-100% or near-0% accuracy without demonstrating consistent logical reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors acknowledge the imbalance as a limitation and attribute the frequent 100% or 0% accuracy to it.

evidence_standards.name: Human label validation
evidence_standards.detail: Surge crowdworkers checked a random sample of at least 50 examples per task; for tasks submitted in multiple parts, 50 examples were taken from each part and agreement scores averaged. The paper reports percentage agreement. No significance test or variance threshold is stated.

evidence_standards.name: Evaluation across model scales and series
evidence_standards.detail: The paper examines trends across model sizes and model series spanning about 10^18 to 10^23 training FLOPs, and uses private Anthropic and DeepMind series as held-out evaluations. It describes prize-winning tasks as appearing to robustly demonstrate inverse scaling, but states no statistical test, confidence interval, or numerical threshold for a real difference.

evidence_standards.name: Prompting settings used for reported results
evidence_standards.detail: The paper evaluates zero-shot and few-shot settings. Few-shot evaluations range from 1 to 72 examples, or the context-length limit if smaller; figures in the task section show zero-shot results. No decoding parameters are specified in the provided text.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared at equivalent target pre-training loss (quality) and inference demand; the paper compares total FLOPs, parameter count, and training-token count.

metrics.name: Pre-training cross-entropy loss
metrics.caveat: Used as a proxy for downstream quality; the paper also evaluates downstream tasks with the Evaluation Gauntlet and reports that loss and Gauntlet Average are tightly correlated.

metrics.name: Category-specific Gauntlet averages
metrics.caveat: The paper says these are less consistently correlated with data and model size because categories have fewer tasks and many tasks show little improvement over random baseline for smaller models; it also reports the overall Gauntlet Average.

metrics.name: Training and inference FLOPs
metrics.caveat: The FLOP-only analysis does not capture differences in hardware utilization and cost per FLOP; the paper also estimates real-world costs using utilization and hardware-cost assumptions.

metrics.name: Estimated real-world training plus inference cost

controls.name: Scaling-law fit using only runs at or below 100 tokens per parameter
controls.detail: The paper compares fits from progressively larger training-data subsets, beginning with runs at or below 100 tokens per parameter and extending to all data, using the described fitting procedure.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether fitting only typical token-to-parameter ratios changes the extrapolated scaling curve; the paper finds that this restricted fit overestimates the impact of additional training data at extreme ratios.

confounds.name: Pre-training loss improvements may not reflect downstream quality improvements
confounds.detail: The headline claim that longer training improves model quality could appear in loss without corresponding downstream-task gains.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate the models on the Evaluation Gauntlet and report that Gauntlet Average improves with tokens per parameter and is tightly correlated with loss.

confounds.name: Models may saturate at extreme training durations or smaller models may have a critical size below which more data cannot help
confounds.detail: The apparent benefit of more tokens per parameter might stop at a saturation point, or small models might fail to continue improving with additional training.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure loss and Gauntlet performance across token-to-parameter ratios; report no evidence of saturation up to 10,000 tokens per parameter for the 150M model and up to 1,000 for larger models, while noting that further testing is needed.

datasets.name: AR (Associative Recall)
datasets.eval_protocol: Single-query associative recall with sequence length L=2N_f+1; report recall accuracy. The paper varies task and model dimensions but does not specify an evaluation split or trial count.

datasets.name: MQAR (Multi-Query Associative Recall)
datasets.eval_protocol: Each sequence has N_f non-repeating key-value facts in a context of 2N_f tokens, followed by N_f queries that repeat context keys; remaining positions are padding, randomly sampled from the full vocabulary following the original implementation. The vocabulary is divided evenly into key and value tokens. Report recall accuracy; the paper does not specify an evaluation split or trial count.

metrics.name: Recall accuracy
metrics.caveat: Accuracy grids use best-of-seeds results, so they measure model capacity—the existence of a recall solution—rather than the probability of finding one through optimization.

controls.name: Conv1D-removal ablation
controls.detail: Compare a simplified Mamba block containing an SSM and a length-2 Conv1D with the block after removing the Conv1D.
controls.rules_out: That the SSM alone is sufficient for recall; recall is nearly perfect with the Conv1D and fails when it is removed, supporting the importance of the copy-and-shift operation.

confounds.name: Optimization failure rather than limited model capacity
confounds.detail: Low recall could reflect failure to find a solution during training, rather than insufficient representational capacity.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Train with multiple random seeds and report best-of-seeds accuracy, which the paper uses to assess whether a recall solution exists; the number of seeds is not specified.

confounds.name: Equivalent parameterizations obscure the proposed circuit in learned weights
confounds.detail: Orthogonal transformations can change individual weights while preserving the same recall computation, so a mismatch with the circuit's specific weights would not by itself refute the mechanism.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Analyze transformation-invariant effective operators G_vv and G_kq, and project the hidden state back into vocabulary space using the stated hidden-state inversion; the paper reports patterns consistent with the proposed circuit.

evidence_standards.name: Multiple random seeds; best-of-seeds accuracy
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports the best accuracy across multiple seeds to assess capacity. It does not specify the seed count or report a statistical test, confidence interval, or variance-based criterion for deciding that differences are real.

metrics.name: Downstream accuracy
metrics.caveat: Multiple-choice benchmarks have nonzero random accuracy, and ambiguous or incorrectly labeled examples can prevent a perfect-accuracy ceiling. The paper normalizes multiple-choice accuracy against estimated random accuracy and proposes a less-than-perfect ceiling extension in Appendix L.

metrics.name: RMSE
metrics.caveat: A good fit on training data need not imply accurate extrapolation; the paper reports held-out prediction errors alongside training fit statistics.

metrics.name: R²
metrics.caveat: A good fit on training data need not imply accurate extrapolation; the paper reports held-out prediction errors alongside training fit statistics.

metrics.name: Log-probability, evaluation loss, and Brier Score
metrics.caveat: Their strong fit to downstream accuracy does not guarantee that a two-stage method extrapolates accurately; the paper compares two-stage held-out predictions against direct approaches.

metrics.name: Negative log-likelihood (NLL)
metrics.caveat: A proxy can fit downstream accuracy yet yield worse extrapolation in a two-stage method; the paper reports held-out prediction errors for the two-stage approaches.

confounds.name: The scaling trend might be specific to the primary pretraining data mixture
confounds.detail: A trend observed with one data mixture might not hold with a different composition.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Train a suite with C4 instead of the primary mixture at TPR 20 and evaluate downstream scaling; the paper reports good fits on eight tasks, while noting code and math performance is near random.

confounds.name: Poor two-stage results might reflect the choice of proxy metric
confounds.detail: An unsuitable proxy could make two-stage prediction look worse even if the approach itself were adequate.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure accuracy relationships for log-probability, evaluation loss, and Brier Score, finding similar fit quality (R² > 0.95); then use NLL for the two-stage comparison and compare held-out predictions.

confounds.name: Random-choice performance could distort the apparent accuracy scaling
confounds.detail: Multiple-choice accuracy has a nonzero random-performance floor.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Estimate random accuracy from 10 small models below 1×10^17 FLOPs and normalize accuracy as (Q−Q_random)/(1−Q_random).

confounds.name: Ambiguous or incorrectly labeled benchmark examples may prevent perfect accuracy
confounds.detail: A less-than-perfect benchmark ceiling could make a model assuming a ceiling of one misrepresent scaling.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in the main analysis; Appendix L proposes an extension that models a less-than-perfect accuracy ceiling.

evidence_standards.name: Held-out compute extrapolation for power law and BNSL
evidence_standards.detail: Fit on runs from 3×10^18 to 6×10^21 FLOPs and evaluate on larger held-out runs; exclude runs less than 5 percentage points above random performance when fitting Equation 2. Report MAE and MRE on validation.

evidence_standards.name: Held-out validation across token-to-parameter ratios
evidence_standards.detail: For Equation 4, hold out all runs above 6×10^21 FLOPs or at the largest TPR (160), fit on the remaining data using Huber loss with δ=1e-3, and report train and validation MAE and MRE.

evidence_standards.name: Held-out validation for repeated-sampling predictions
evidence_standards.detail: For Equation 5, fit on HumanEval experiments below 6×10^21 FLOPs and with k≤32, validate on the remaining data, and report train and validation MAE and MRE.

evidence_standards.name: Two-stage versus direct prediction comparison
evidence_standards.detail: Fit on data up to 6×10^21 FLOPs and validate above that threshold; report MRE, MAE, RMSE, and R², with means and standard deviations across benchmarks in Table 4.

baselines.name: Qwen3-14B-Base without CPT
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper states that the base model is Qwen3-14B-Base and that all models use the same evaluation setting.

baselines.name: RS-CPT
baselines.fair_comparison: Random data sampling; the paper states that all models use the same evaluation setting and identifies Qwen3-14B-Base as the base model.

baselines.name: LPS-CPT
baselines.fair_comparison: Samples low-PPL data below the optimal PPL range derived by DOS; the paper states that all models use the same evaluation setting and identifies Qwen3-14B-Base as the base model.

baselines.name: HPS-CPT
baselines.fair_comparison: Samples high-PPL data above the optimal PPL range derived by DOS; the paper states that all models use the same evaluation setting and identifies Qwen3-14B-Base as the base model.

controls.name: Qwen3-14B-Base without CPT
controls.detail: The unmodified base model is evaluated alongside the CPT conditions.
controls.rules_out: A comparison against this reference shows whether performance differs from the base model without CPT.

controls.name: RS-CPT random data sampling
controls.detail: CPT using randomly sampled data.
controls.rules_out: A comparison against random-sampling CPT tests whether the result is explained by CPT with a random data subset rather than DOS-guided selection.

confounds.name: The medical gains come at the cost of forgetting general-domain knowledge
confounds.detail: Medical performance could improve while general capabilities deteriorate.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on general-domain CEVAL, CMMLU, and MMLU; the paper reports the DOS average as 84.16, matching the base model's 84.16.

confounds.name: The fitted scaling law only fits its training points rather than generalizing to unseen configurations
confounds.detail: The observed fit could reflect interpolation or overfitting to the subsets used to fit the law.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate predictions on an independent validation set disjoint from fitting data, with configurations from the same underlying distribution but different PPL profiles.

evidence_standards.name: Scaling-law fit and validation split
evidence_standards.detail: Use 90% of the bootstrap-sampled PubMed subsets to fit the scaling curve and 10% for validation; the paper also describes an independent validation set disjoint from fitting data. It reports no seeds, statistical test, or numerical threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: WMT-17 en-de
datasets.eval_protocol: Finetunes on 3B tokens; also uses randomly sampled portions of 6M and 31M tokens. Reports BLEU and downstream cross-entropy; COMET results are provided in the appendix. The evaluation split and scoring details beyond the named metrics are not specified.

datasets.name: WMT-15 en-fr
datasets.eval_protocol: Finetunes on 21B tokens; also uses randomly sampled portions of 42M and 210M tokens. Reports BLEU and downstream cross-entropy; COMET results are provided in the appendix. The evaluation split and scoring details beyond the named metrics are not specified.

datasets.name: WMT-16 en-ro
datasets.eval_protocol: Finetunes on 312M tokens; also uses randomly sampled portions of 625K and 3M tokens. Reports BLEU and downstream cross-entropy; COMET results are provided in the appendix. The evaluation split and scoring details beyond the named metrics are not specified.

datasets.name: SuperGLUE
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses models pretrained on en-MC4 and finetuned on BoolQ, MultiRC, COPA, ReCoRD, and RTE to examine scaling on question answering, reasoning, reading comprehension, and textual entailment. Per-task splits, scoring rules, and other evaluation details are not specified in the provided text.

baselines.name: Non-pretrained, randomly initialized model trained directly on the task dataset
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same translation task and finetuning dataset portions as the pretrained models; the text does not specify further controls for the comparison.

metrics.name: BLEU
metrics.caveat: Translation scores can fluctuate or worsen as pretraining data grows when the pretraining data is insufficiently aligned, even while downstream cross-entropy improves. The paper reports cross-entropy alongside BLEU and also reports COMET results.

metrics.name: COMET
metrics.caveat: The paper says its COMET results show observations similar to BLEU, including non-monotonic behavior in some less-aligned settings; it reports downstream cross-entropy alongside translation-quality scores.

metrics.name: Downstream cross-entropy
metrics.caveat: It can improve monotonically even when translation quality fluctuates or worsens, so it is not always a reliable proxy for task performance. The paper reports translation-quality metrics such as BLEU and COMET alongside it.

controls.name: Non-pretrained, randomly initialized model trained directly on the task dataset
controls.detail: A randomly initialized model is trained directly on the translation task data; the paper plots this reference for different finetuning dataset sizes.
controls.rules_out: A comparison against this reference indicates whether pretraining improves on direct training with the available task data.

confounds.name: BLEU non-monotonicity is caused by the brevity penalty rather than n-gram precision
confounds.detail: A changing brevity penalty could account for the observed fluctuations in BLEU as pretraining data grows.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures the BLEU brevity penalty and reports it is 1 in all experiments, attributing the non-monotonic behavior to the n-gram precision term.

confounds.name: Cross-entropy improvement is mistaken for improved translation quality
confounds.detail: Downstream cross-entropy can improve monotonically even in cases where translation scores fluctuate or decline, so a cross-entropy-only result could appear positive without better translation quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures and reports translation-quality scores, including BLEU and COMET, alongside downstream cross-entropy and shows cases where their trends differ.

evidence_standards.name: Held-out prediction evaluation for fitted scaling laws
evidence_standards.detail: Fits the scaling-law coefficients using the first four data points requiring the least pretraining data and holds out the remaining points to evaluate prediction accuracy. Uses Huber loss with δ=0.1 for translation scores and δ=1e-3 for downstream cross-entropy, optimized with L-BFGS; no seed-based variance or statistical significance rule is specified.

datasets.name: C4
datasets.eval_protocol: Test loss on 1% of the original C4 dataset; text overlapping with the training set was removed by deduplication. Context window 1024; loss is cross-entropy in nats averaged over tokens in a context.

datasets.name: Code data (in-domain test set)
datasets.eval_protocol: Test loss on code data following the same distribution as the training data; code is 10% of the full training data. Context window 4096; each training batch contained about 4M tokens. No test split or trial count is specified.

datasets.name: Private Chinese data (out-of-domain test set)
datasets.eval_protocol: Test loss on private Chinese data described as rare in the training data and out of domain. Context window 4096; each training batch contained about 4M tokens. No split or trial count is specified.

metrics.name: Test loss (cross-entropy loss in nats averaged over tokens in a context)
metrics.caveat: Out-of-domain loss trajectories can fluctuate significantly, and early-stage predictions can be inaccurate due to warm-up and a large prediction multiplier; the paper also compares overall trajectory trends and final converged loss values.
